items.text: Thank you, Madam Chair, and also just
a signal to you, Madam Chair, that I intend to just ask one question around the amendment
to Part 3, and I’ve got a couple of questions—maybe I can have a back and forth with the
Minister—on Part 4 before moving on to subsequent sections.
So we’re looking at clause 37, “New sections 89A to 89 E”. We’re going to start with
that one. I just have one question for the Minister in the chair, the Hon James Meager,
which is: considering when we’re looking at 89A, which talks about chief executives or
boards, as the Minister would undoubtedly know, that school boards are considered under
that category, but in a situation where a school board is either disestablished due to
conversion from a State or State-integrated to a charter school, how would—for example,
89C in terms of redundancy payment—work for those who are no longer working in a
department or interdepartmental venture in those sort of cases? Noting that school boards
are still considered an active part in 89A, because should school boards not be included,
we would see a similar line as what we see in clause 38, new section 94B(1), where the
school board has been specifically excluded? If school boards are included, how would it
work in terms of its interactions with the provisions in the Education and Training Act
regarding charter schools and regarding conversion?
That’s my first question to the Minister. I’m hearing that the Minister is getting some
advice around that.

items.speaker: CHAIRPERSON
items.text: The Minister’s going to answer it straight off.
Hon JAMES MEAGER (Minister for Hunting and Fishing) ( 20:59): Thank you,
Madam Chair. I apologise, the member may have missed the exchange with Camilla
Belich earlier, but clause 37 is a lift and shift from Schedule 8, from memory. It just
replicates clauses 7 to—oh, how’s my memory; 7 to 11 in Schedule 8.
Hey, there you go: clause 47(3) of the bill points to the repealing of clauses 7 to 11 in
Schedule 8, and what clause 37 does is it repeats those clauses but puts them in the body
of the bill, so there’s no change to the existing law. However, the existing law would
apply to entities under this arrangement; that would be what would apply after this bill
passes. Nothing changes in that sense.
Just to the member’s second point, around school boards, school boards are Crown
entities, so they wouldn’t be captured by the Public Service Act.

items.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN
items.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. Thank you,
Minister. On the amendment to Part 4, I want to speak to the diversity inclusion part. The
first question to the Minister: has the Minister, as part of compiling this bill, received any
feedback from the Ministry for Ethnic Communities or the Ministry for Pacific Peoples
around the removal of diversity and inclusiveness in the workforce policy intent? I’m just
checking.
Hon PRIYANCA RADHAKRISHNAN (Labour) ( 21:01): Thank you, Madam
Chair. My series of questions are also related to clause 39, the repeal of 97(2)(e), but
focusing on the workplace diversity and inclusion aspects of it.
I did ask the Minister a couple of questions previously during this committee stage, in
terms of the evidence or the problem definition: what is this trying to fix and where is the
evidence that appointments are being made not based on merit? I didn’t get any response
17 Feb 2026 Bills 17529
there. In fact, what I got from the Minister, and I’ve just checked the Hansard, was
basically his claim that I said the only way that people of different ethnicities or genders
or sexuality can gain their place in the system is by being put there by virtue of a list or a
tick-box. I find that very offensive, because that is not what I said, and I want to set the
record straight there.
The Minister then went on to say that the Government’s expectation is that the Public
Service will be made up of individuals who are competent, capable, and intelligent
people, and “if we appoint competent, capable, intelligent people, we will get people from
across the spectrum.” I have a number of questions for the Minister based on this. I will
just preface that, though, with the point that the Disabled Persons Assembly has made.
This is not just about ethnicity quotas, as the Minister seemed to interpret my question to
be. The Disabled Persons Assembly, for example, has said that these changes will make
it harder for disabled job applicants to overcome discriminatory barriers when seeking
employment within the public sector. The Parents of Vision Impaired (NZ) has said that
it moves towards marginalising disabled communities in decision-making processes. This
hasn’t come from nowhere; there’s been a whole programme of change since 2017.
I asked the Minister for some evidence that things have changed for the better as a
result of changes made in 2017 and these particular sections of the Public Service Act
2020 that he’s proposing to repeal, but he couldn’t give me any. I will share that, for
Asians, for example, workforce participation went up from 3.3 percent in 2000 to 9.4
percent in 2017—a very, very short change or a very slow improvement in 17 years—and
then went up to 13.4 percent in 2020, in just three years, so there is the evidence that it is
working.
Now, the questions that I have for the Minister, and I do echo the question by Dr

items.speaker: Lawrence Xu-Nan
items.text: what was the advice, if any, that was provided on this by population
agencies like the Ministry for Ethnic Communities, the Ministry for Pacific Peoples, or—I
will add to that—Whaikaha, the Ministry of Disabled People? I’d also like to know what
advice the Minister has received on the impact that these changes will have on workforce
diversity in the Public Service. I do have a few more questions to come, too, Minister, but
perhaps we could start with these.
I will also put this in the context of the royal commission of inquiry, where the
commission found, specifically, the need for the Public Service to improve workforce
diversity to ensure that they can actually be responsive towards all communities in New
Zealand and build trust with those communities. That was a specific point in a few of the
royal commission’s recommendations. We see, globally, trust in institutions declining.
What advice has the Minister received on the impact of these changes when it comes to
increasing or decreasing trust from these specific communities who are being impacted
by this change?
Hon JAMES MEAGER (Minister for Hunting and Fishing) ( 21:05): Thank you,
Madam Chair. I’ll avoid going back and relitigating—you know, the member’s desire to
try and hunt down particular individuals appointed to positions who particular individual
members of Parliament might think not to be suitable for the job. I don’t think that’s a
helpful way of talking about our public sector leaders, but I will address the point around
the impact on the disabled community. I’ll draw the member’s attention to section 73 of
the principal Act. Section 73 requires public sector employers to operate employment
policies that recognise the employment requirements of people with disabilities. That is
an obligation for the public sector to undertake and does not change with this bill.
17530 Bills 17 Feb 2026
In terms of the question around advice received on whether or not we anticipate a
change in, I guess, what is the demographic make-up, I would assume not. I think that
goes back to the point we made earlier, which is that we expect the public sector to be
made up of highly competent, intelligent, capable people. Those people exist across all
facets of life, and if we are hiring those people then I would expect—whether that comes
from an ethnic minority or a particular gender minority or any other kind of demographic;
you might want to split it—that those people are able to be identified, because they exist
in those communities in abundance. We don’t think that this will have a significant
change—or any change, really—from the removal of the list of matters in section 97,
which clause 39 removes, because we are, of course, talking about the Government
Workforce Policy Statement. I outlined to Camilla Belich, before, the reasons why we
think this is the right thing to do.
I’ll just note that the advice in front of me does say that over the last decade, including
prior to the changes made in the 2020 Act, we have seen significant positive upward
trends in ethnic and gender and minority representation across the board. I suspect it has
more to do with our society’s desire to see a workforce which is representative of New
Zealand. For us, that means a workforce which represents the talents, skills, and
competency across all parts of society. We expect that to continue. Whether you are from
Timaru or Takapuna or Te Atatū or Tauranga or Hamilton, we expect competent people
to be appointed to these positions.

through the areas that they are.
I think we’ve moved on to the schedules now, which have not been covered to date.
There are a couple of questions I have for the Minister around the schedules, and then I
do think it is important that we at least cover the long-term insights briefings, which are
further along in the schedules, around Schedule 6. That would be my request: to be able

My initial questions are around the cost recovery in clause 43, and that’s an
amendment to Schedule 3. Essentially, as I understand it, the commissioner is able to
undertake certain inquiries and investigations into the public sector, and also recover costs
from them. There doesn’t seem to be a limit on that listed here, and so I want to know, as
the Minister is aware— and we’ve traversed that there are a few lift and shift provisions
here. I just wanted to check: is this a lift and shift provision, and even regardless of
whether it’s new or a lift and shift provision, I ask whether there is any ability for agencies
to agree or monitor the cost of inquiries which the commissioner can do into that
department. As members will know, sometimes these can be quite expensive and, for
17 Feb 2026 Bills 17531
smaller agencies, it might be important to be able to have an idea of the costs. I appreciate
it that colleagues from the other side are always keen to make sure that departments are
living within their means, and this provision doesn’t have that much detail on it.
The other question that I had is about where there’s a whole power here in new clause
5A in Schedule 3, in clause 43, and it’s also referred to in new clause 4(2A) in Schedule
3, also in clause 43, that looks towards performance improvement reviews. The thing that

items.speaker: I wanted to know is
items.text: is the Public Service Commissioner being given any additional
resources—so it’s kind of the opposite of my last question. There are quite a few powers
that they have to be able to conduct performance reviews of agencies. I think that’s an
appropriate role for the Public Service Commissioner to have, but are there any additional
resources going to be provided to the Public Service Commissioner to allow that to occur?
In the schedule that we haven’t covered yet, there are quite substantial powers that the
Public Service Commissioner has, and probably the third point I’d make on this before
moving on is that it has quite a significant role in relation to identification of specific
vendors, where it may provide guidance to existing Public Service agencies. I wanted to
know the mischief of that, as well. Obviously, there will be particular vendors that they
will want to provide guidance for, and they perhaps want a consistency of approach in the
public sector in relation to specific vendors, but I do think that that is important.
I do have questions in relation to the long-term insights briefing, but I’ll just see if the
Minister would like those questions now or if he is able to address the initial questions.
Hon JAMES MEAGER (Minister for Hunting and Fishing) ( 21:13): Thank you,
Madam Chair. A couple of questions around powers for investigations and inquiries. The
first one was whether this is a lift and shift or a new power. It’s kind of somewhere in the
middle; it codifies existing practice, which, I’m advised, is relatively well accepted, so it
just provides some legislative framework for that practice, including the cost recovery
around that.
The second question is around the actual undertaking of investigations, and this goes
to clause 43(7). The Public Service Commissioner already conducts a number of these
investigations within baseline. This just provides a clearer mandate for those
investigations and perhaps a bit more specificity on them.
Just to round out the question from Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan that I didn’t get to before,
he asked a question around whether or not the Ministry for Ethnic Communities and the
Ministry for Pacific Peoples and others had provided feedback. Yes, the feedback was
taken into account when drafting the legislation, and that is noted in the regulatory impact
statement.
CAMILLA BELICH (Labour) ( 21:14): Thank you, Madam Chair. I did, as noted
before, have some questions around the long-term insights briefings. Essentially, what
this bill is doing, as I understand it—and this is in relation to Schedule 6—at the moment,
I think we have about 34 long-term insights briefings which are created, and one of the
functions is that Parliament actually has a better idea of being able to scrutinise the
different agencies on what they intend to do long term.
Now, this takes it right back to one single long-term insights briefing, which is a
significant change. We heard at select committee that the long-term insights briefing
would be able to look across a number of different portfolios; it’s meant to be created by
the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet (DPMC). We did have a number of
submissions on this at select committee, and the submissions were generally in favour of,
if I recall correctly, keeping the long-term insights briefings, because of how valuable
they were to certain members of the community. In fact, there was a submission given by
17532 Bills 17 Feb 2026
the Clerk of the House that indicated that, in his view, the long-term insights briefings as
they are currently collated and put forward to the House actually do assist the House in
scrutinising. What I wanted to know from the Minister is: what checks and balances will
there be in place to ensure that the now single long-term insights briefing from DPMC
truly does reflect the type of content that we were getting from the 34 different long-term
insights briefings?
Additionally, I put some amendments on the Table—I’m sure my colleague Francisco
Hernandez may have as well—around whether there is perhaps a better balance that we
could strike in relation to going from, I think, 34 down to one. I’ve listed some for
potential agencies in my amendment to be covered by long-term insights briefings. I think
this is quite a significant change in terms of how we think about issues long term. I
wondered what other direction could be given to agencies to allow that long-term thinking
to occur. We do often find with agencies, when we’re looking at the Estimates and we’re
looking at the annual reviews, that we’re looking very much in the short term. There is a
need, and it should be noted that the infrastructure plan that the Minister’s Government
announced did look towards some of this long-term decision-making that I understand
the report indicates is incumbent upon New Zealand to make.
One of the things that submitters were concerned about is how this will actually
work—in terms of such a significant reduction in the long-term insights briefings—and
what, really, we can expect the guidance to be to the public sector to make sure they are
considering the long-term challenges that face New Zealand, in the absence of a
requirement to provide a long-term insights briefing. Of course, I think this is something
that parliamentarians in select committees should also note. We can open briefings into
any issue that we want. That, I think, might be something the Minister wants to comment
on as well, in terms of making sure that Parliament actually has that long-term view. I
think submitters—and I agree with them—are right to think that we are losing some long-
term strategic focus by the loss of these long-term insights briefings.
Hon JAMES MEAGER (Minister for Hunting and Fishing) ( 21:18): Thank you,
Madam Chair. The member Camilla Belich, without wanting to get too much into legal
parlance or court phrase, asked and answered her own question around views on long-
term insights briefing. Essentially, just to go to the amendments, I understand the desire
to try and meet a balance between 34 and one large one which covers multiple areas and
multiple topics, whether it’s 20 or 19 or 10; there’s probably no one, magic number. I
guess the idea behind this is to try and reduce as much as possible the duplication and the
repeated resource and try and sharpen the focus on those long-term insights briefings to
fit with the priorities of the Government of the day, which is why this would come through
the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet in conjunction with all these other
departments. While I acknowledge the amendments, we won’t be supporting them.
To the question around stewardship and taking long-term views and what guarantees
we can have that the public sector will continue to look at the long-term impacts of
Government policy, we had this discussion, I think, right at the top of the debate when
we started the committee stage; we had quite a lengthy discussion around long-termism
and active citizenship and some of the ways that Governments can take long-term views.
Members across the House can agree on the long-term priorities or projects or 30-year
infrastructure plans or whatever it might be that we ended up agreeing on. I pointed to
some provisions around requirements for the public sector to take that stewardship role
and that long-term role which is already existing in the Act. That should provide some
reassurance that those long-term views are taken.
17 Feb 2026 Bills 17533
Just, finally, around the value of these long-term insight briefings to select committees,
I would agree that there is some value in some of those briefings, particularly when select
committees use them well and incorporate them into their scrutiny plans. But, as the
member said, select committees have quite a wide-ranging range of powers to initiate
their own briefings and inquiries and request documents and information from
departments, and so if there is a desire from select committees to have that information
available to fit with the priorities of their scrutiny plan, then I’m sure the Parliament
would encourage select committees to take those steps.
I think one thing that would be good for select committees to consider, perhaps as we
wrap up this section and as they look to wrap up their work programme for the year, is
that we report on our scrutiny activities as select committees, but perhaps before the
Parliament rises, select committees consider setting out some guidance for future select
committees about how they may want to manage or adopt or adapt a future scrutiny plan.
I recall that when we came into this Parliament, scrutiny plans were quite new, and we
were kind of making them up on the fly and we had no guidance or sort of templates from
previous select committees. I think that would be a good thing to do—for one select
committee to leave a bit of a legacy for the next one to carry on the focus of that particular
scrutiny plan, with the ability to change it.

FINANCE 
Question No. 1 
CAMERON BREWER (National—Upper Harbour) ( 14:02) to the Minister of 
Finance: What is the Treasury’s recommended ceiling for New Zealand’s net core Crown 
debt? 
Hon NICOLA WILLIS (Minister of Finance) ( 14:02): In 2022, the Treasury 
recommended some fiscal rules to the Government, including a ceiling for net core Crown 
debt. The idea is to maintain net debt at a prudent level while providing headroom to 
respond to economic shocks and natural disasters. After thorough analysis and modelling, 
Treasury’s recommendation was for a net core Crown debt ceiling of 50 percent of GDP. 
Finance Minister Grant Robertson accepted that recommendation, and so have I. The 
ceiling is getting close. Net core Crown debt is expected to rise to 46.9 percent in the 
2028-29 fiscal year, before beginning to fall. In public forums, Treasury’s secretary, Iain 
Rennie, has frequently discussed the need to bend the public debt curve down, as is the

Hon BROOKE VAN VELDEN:  Today is a great day for New Zealand’s labour 
market. With this bill, we are delivering on our promise to restore confidence, drive 
growth, and modernise our employment relations framework for a new era. This bill is 
about solutions. It tackles four key areas that have been holding our economy back. Let 
me be clear about what we are fixing and how.  
Firstly, this bill provides greater certainty for contracting parties. Contractors play an 
important role in New Zealand’s economy and society. Businesses and workers have 
faced uncertainty about who is an employee and who is a contractor, which has prevented 
workers from accessing flexible contracting opportunities that stifle innovation and 
growth. This bill introduces a gateway test that creates an exclusion from the definition 
of employee, consisting of criteria that represent characteristics of clear-cut contracting 
arrangements. This provides businesses with a clearer and more efficient test to determine 
whether a worker is a contractor or an employee. 
If the worker does not meet the criteria, they can be assessed under the existing 
common law test. This test gives legal weight to the intention of contracting parties; 
protects genuine contracting arrangements, including modern platform-based 
arrangements; and allows businesses and workers to move forward with confidence 
knowing where they stand. 
Secondly, this bill rebalances the personal grievance settings. In recent years, the 
amount of remedies awarded have increased and remedy reductions for employee 
misconduct have declined, leaving employers with greater liability even in serious cases. 
This imbalance is unfair and does not improve workplace conduct. This bill strengthens 
the consideration of, and accountability for, the employee’s behaviour in the personal 
grievance process. It does this by removing an employee’s eligibility for all remedies if 
their behaviour amounts to serious misconduct, and removing eligibility for reinstatement 
and compensation for hurt and humiliation if they have contributed to the situation that 
led to that personal grievance. 
17 Feb 2026 Bills 17471 
 
It also makes the personal grievance process less demanding for employers by 
requiring the Employment Relations Authority to consider whether the employee 
obstructed the employer’s process, and relaxing the threshold for procedural error.  
Thirdly, this bill introduces a remuneration threshold for eligibility to raise an 
unjustified dismissal personal grievance. Businesses need the confidence to hire and 
manage high-earning, high-impact employees, but the risk of costly, drawn-out personal 
grievance claims has made it harder for businesses to properly reward and take risks on 
talented employees. This is what the remuneration threshold is all about: more high-
earning, high-impact jobs for emerging talent to drive our economy forward. The 
remuneration threshold will be set at $200,000 and be based on a total PAYE income, 
capturing all forms of remuneration such as bonuses and employee shares. This figure 
will be adjusted based on upward movements in average wages every year after 2027. 
Employees will still have the option to contract back into unjustified dismissal 
protections, if they choose to, and there will be a 12-month transition period for high-
earning employees on existing employment agreements.  
Lastly, this bill increases freedom of choice and reduces red tape at the start of 
employment. It does this by revoking what is commonly known as the 30-day rule. This 
will allow employers that are party to collective employment agreements to hire new 
employees on bespoke flexible terms for the first 30 days of employment—reducing 
compliance costs. These terms could include a 90-day trial period, if both parties agree, 
supporting the Government’s intended expansion of the 90-day trials and making hiring 
easier.  
In conclusion, this bill is a win for New Zealand. It is practical, forward-looking, and 
delivers real benefits for businesses and workers alike. We are cutting red tape, restoring 
balance, and setting our labour market and economy up for success. I commend this bill 
to the House.

The bill addresses judgments that the High Court has made that conflict with 
longstanding policy intent for how ACC compensation, and income more broadly, is 
treated in the welfare system. While these judgments highlight inconsistencies between 
legislation and longstanding policy, they do not reflect the principles of a targeted welfare 
system that provides assistance based on need, and they create inequities across ACC 
recipients in the welfare system. The financial and operational impacts of this High Court 
judgment are significant and Cabinet has agreed to amend legislation to confirm the 
longstanding policy intent that underpins the Ministry of Social Development’s (MSD’s) 
approach to charging income, including income from ACC. 
17 Feb 2026 Bills 17509 
 
I acknowledge that retrospective legislation is not standard. However, Parliament is 
entitled to amend legislation in light of judicial decisions and I consider it in the public 
interest for policy intent to be accurately reflected in the law. To be clear: the bill confirms 
longstanding policy intent and operational practice; it does not create new policy or 
change MSD’s treatment of clients in any way. 
The first key change aligns legislation with longstanding policy and practice that 
income is charged against the period it best represents, to ensure MSD charges a person’s 
income accurately against their entitlement. Longstanding policy intends for MSD to 
charge income over a certain period, which is generally the period the person earned or 
became entitled to that income. When charging income for a past period, MSD may find 
that overpayments occurred and recoverable debt should be established.  
Charging income against the period it best represents has been a longstanding policy 
in the way income is treated in the welfare system. This core feature enables MSD to 
charge a person’s income accurately against their entitlement by aligning it with the 
period it relates to. This is important as people can receive income that relates to different 
periods, for many reasons. For example, a person may receive a large interest payment 
that reflects the past year of investment. In this case, charging the payment as a single 
lump sum when the person received the payments may not accurately reflect the period 
the interest best represents. 
In 2024, the Social Security Appeal Authority found MSD did not consider all of the 
relevant factors when exercising its discretion to determine the correct period to charge 
income. The bill addresses the Social Security Appeal Authority decision by amending 
the Social Security Act 2018, so when calculating a person’s weekly income—including 
ACC income—MSD must determine the period the income relates to based only on the 
extent to which a person earned or became entitled to it in that period. If this is not 
possible, MSD must determine the appropriate period to charge that income, having a 
regard to the period for which it was received, acquired, paid, provided, or supplied. 
The key thing here is this change upholds a policy that’s always been in place to 
allocate income against the period it best represents so that a person’s income can 
continue to be charged accurately against their entitlement. 
The second key change relates to the treatment of a person as a non-beneficiary when 
their ACC compensation payment reduces their benefit entitlement to zero for the past 
period. Currently, if a person’s main benefit reduced to zero because of their income, 
longstanding policy intends for MSD to consider the person a non-beneficiary, which of 
course makes sense and which may affect their entitlement to supplementary assistance. 
For example, non-beneficiaries are not entitled to the winter energy payment and are 
subject to income abatement for the accommodation supplement. This is unlike people 
with main beneficiary status who have a greater need for supplementary assistance due to 
their comparatively lower income. 
Assistance must be targeted to those who need it most in our welfare system. This 
policy reflects the principle ensuring people receive financial assistance relative to their 
income levels and are only receiving one form of income support for one need. 
In October 2025, the High Court found that MSD is operating outside of existing 
legislative authority when reassessing a person’s entitlement to supplementary assistance 
after they receive a backdated ACC payment from a past period. This bill addresses the 
High Court decision by amending the Social Security Act 2018 so that when a person 
receives a backdated ACC payment, MSD must review specified supplementary 
assistance granted for that past period and treat the person as a non-beneficiary if their 
17510 Bills 17 Feb 2026 
 
specified benefit reduced to zero. MSD may make changes to the person’s entitlement as 
part of this review. 
This is an important amendment to ensure that when assessing a person’s entitlement 
to supplementary assistance, MSD maintains equitable treatment between people 
receiving ACC payments at the time they earn it compared to payments earned for a past 
period—i.e., a backdating. 
This bill introduces an amendment that has retrospective effect, to ensure the policy 
intent is maintained for both past and prospective cases. Retrospective legislation isn’t 
standard; however, it is an important public interest for this longstanding policy intent to 
be accurately reflected in the law and to mitigate any flow-on financial and operational 
impacts.  
This bill introduces a savings provision to ensure the key changes do not interfere with 
previous or ongoing litigation, reflecting the strong convention that parliamentary 
legislation should not generally interfere with specific cases that are before the courts. 
There are some time constraints in passing this legislation so that we do uphold 
longstanding policy and practice to ensure that income is charged accurately against a 
person’s entitlement, that ACC recipients continue to be treated equitably, and to mitigate 
the fiscal impacts to the Crown and operational impacts to MSD. Can I put my gratitude 
to the House on record for the engagement I’ve had with parties opposite in the interests 
of getting this bill progressed. I commend this bill to the House.
